point: The review is organised around stochasticity, hydraulic modelling, market participation and solution methods, and will compare and criticise the literature against the thesis.
The review extends the earlier specialisation-project reviews rather than running a new systematic search, but still applies quality criteria.
The search follows an adapted backward snowballing approach.
Stochastic modelling pays off in hydropower planning, increasingly so with longer horizons, and arises from inflow, prices and climate variables.
Inflow is among the most important uncertainties because it governs long-term hydropower availability, as recognised since the original SDDP work.
Weather variables such as temperature can also be stochastic, and affect production, water values and demand-driven prices.
Prices are usually modelled as stochastic, yet uncertainty in regulation prices is under-treated and scenario dimensionality limits modelling every price.
Most studies assume price-taking, which suits day-ahead but is less clear in other markets, where price-maker modelling can cut spillage.
Bid volume affects the risk of not being activated in balancing markets, and reserve-usage uncertainty deserves modelling in this thesis.
Prices and inflows are the key uncertain variables, and the number of stochastic variables stays small to avoid dimensionality problems.
Uncertainty must be represented with realistic, transparently constructed data that preserve statistical properties such as correlations.
Reported correlations between prices and inflow differ across studies, so an absence of correlation should not be read as no relationship.
Scenario trees are built through common steps, with varying data length and node counts that shape computational effort and tree quality.
Input data granularity differs between studies, and should be chosen to fit the purpose and scope of the analysis.
Non-convex unit commitment and generation characteristics must be modelled to avoid overestimating reserve capacity sales when co-optimising energy and reserves.
Non-convexities matter at all horizons and with more renewables, though high-head Norwegian plants make head effects smaller than elsewhere.
Production function representation is a trade-off between accuracy and computational burden that should match the model purpose.
The subsection examines which energy and reserve market combinations have been studied and whether from an investment perspective.
Results from multi-market studies are context-dependent and not directly comparable or generalisable across regions, cases and input assumptions.
Multi-market bidding is either coordinated or sequential, and coordinated optimisation is the more commonly studied.
Day-ahead plus intraday participation adds little value and is rarely studied, while reserve markets attract increasing attention.
Adding aFRR participation raises profit by amounts ranging from about one percent to a quarter, depending on country and bidding approach.
Combining day-ahead with symmetric reserves raised profit by several percent and shifted production toward fewer full-load hours.
Coordinated bidding earns more than sequential bidding, both beat energy-only, and withholding capacity can pay off, which matters for market design.
With mFRR as balancing market, gains were far smaller but coordination still won, and its value grows with uncertainty.
Multi-market participation seen from an investment perspective is little explored, leaving room for the thesis to add this dimension.
The subsection introduces deterministic equivalent, SDP and SDDP as solution methods for multistage stochastic hydropower planning.
Deterministic equivalent formulations with short horizons and MILP can handle realistic multi-market scheduling despite dimensionality limits.
SDP suits smaller systems needing accurate non-convex representation, usually through binaries in stage problems, and ignoring binaries overestimates reserve ability.
SDDP overcomes the dimensionality limit of SDP and is the state-of-the-art for medium-term scheduling in hydro-dominated systems.
SDDP avoids state discretisation by building cutting-plane approximations, which cut computation and gave rapid convergence in a large application.
Several SDDP extensions improved risk handling, water values and policy quality, but none focused on multiple electricity markets.
Hybrid SDP/SDDP studies added multi-market participation, but investment implications such as capacity upgrades remain largely unexplored with SDDP.
The review shows stochasticity, multi-market participation and non-convexity matter, with possible implications for long-term upgrade investments.
A gap remains in evaluating comprehensive market participation for hydropower upgrades, which the thesis addresses through its research questions.
The thesis contributes an SDDP framework with stochastic inflow and prices, a comprehensive market set and an investment perspective.
